prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Document units:
U0088: For example, the ATM system can plan and control pushback times based on scheduled takeoff times and with consideration of runway queue management, without needing to provide a closed trajectory on the surface.
U0089: However, MBT is compatible with TBO concepts that do envision a closed trajectory on the surface such as [3].
U0090: What is most important for MBT, from the surface point of view, is exchange of the necessary data to provide an interface between surface and en route operations and an assigned trajectory that is consistent with a surface management plan that delivers expected surface event times that impact airborne operations [1].
U0091: For example, reliable takeoff and landing time predictions, runway assignments, and inclusion of the departure and arrival transitions in the assigned trajectory support coordination between en route and surface environments.
U0092: Surface operations will be very diverse for different types of users, further motivating treating MBT ground operations as a separate research topic.
U0093: Emergent users may share traditional airports or operate to/from alternative sites.
U0094: Space vehicles operate from special launch and recovery sites and often have no surface movements.
U0095: Rotorcraft are able to “air taxi” and therefore are not constrained by taxiways and do not require runways. 1.6.2 Traffic Flow Management Traffic flow management is separate from the MBT concept.
U0096: TFM is responsible for selecting traffic management initiatives (TMIs), which impose constraints on trajectories.
U0097: The MBT concept addresses the assignment of trajectories that are compliant with all TMIs, the modification of assigned trajectories as constraints change, and the satisfaction of the constraints as aircraft follow the assigned trajectories.
U0098: Improved predictability resulting from MBT will allow TFM to select more-effective TMIs.
U0099: In the near-term, GDPs and AFPs will continue to function as they presently do.
U0100: In the longer-term environment, GDPs/AFPs will move from controlling through the use of an Expect Departure Clearance Time (EDCT) constraining the departure time to enforcement of the CTA at the limited resource as a time constraint on the assigned trajectory.
U0101: The operator will have flexibility to determine when the aircraft takes off, depending on how fast or slow it wants to fly to conform with the CTA and how the takeoff time will affect other constraints.
U0102: Mile-in-trail and minute-in-trail (MINIT) restrictions will be reduced in the near term and eventually eliminated as unnecessary when flights are following 4DTs that include time-based constraints where necessary.
U0103: Increased use of self-separation techniques (e.g., A-IM) will allow efficient management of aircraft merging to a runway or other constrained airspace resource, without needing to repeatedly update time constraints in the assigned trajectories in response to residual uncertainty.
U0104: By keeping all flights on closed trajectories that are de-conflicted over at least the next 30 minutes, MBT may increase sector capacities.
U0105: Uncertainty, which MBT will reduce, hampers current TFM performance.
U0106: However, many TFM processes take advantage of the flexibility in current operations.
U0107: In any TBO environment, if aircraft are more predictable and are scheduled accordingly, the reduction in uncertainty may be accompanied by a reduction in flexibility.
U0108: However, some residual uncertainty will persist, creating the possibility that the TFM system might be more fragile to the remaining uncertainty.
U0109: One area in which research will be required to validate the MBT concept is how TFM must adjust to the tradeoff between uncertainty and flexibility to achieve the anticipated TFM benefits.
U0110: For example, if TFM continues to be conservative and initially absorb less delay than it expects will be required, to leave flexibility to fill an empty slot caused by another flight being late, then most flights will need their assigned trajectories to be updated, potentially multiple times, as the TFM system “releases” more and more of the expected necessary delay to the flights.
U0111: How will this affect predictability and MBT benefits? 1.7 Document Structure The remainder of this document is organized as follows:  Section 2 defines several terms that are key to the MBT ConOps.  Section 3 describes the trajectory negotiation process.  Section 4 presents the trajectory constraint language.  Section 5 describes several elements of the MBT concept.  Section 6 provides use cases that illustrate the MBT concept.  Section 7 summarizes the MBT benefit mechanisms.  Section 8 summarizes expected changes in roles and responsibilities in the NAS due to MBT.  Section 9 provides a summary of the MBT concept. 2.
